title: Payments at an official’s request, and gifts
question: Who paid money to a third party because a supervisor or mayor asked, who gave the official gifts or travel, and did those payors and givers have business before that official?
finding: Supervisors and mayors on the roster reported $12.7 million paid to third parties at their request and $7.8 million given to ballot committees at their request (the two together, most: Edwin Lee $11.3 million, Daniel Lurie $3.8 million, London N. Breed $1.7 million), and $598,725 in gifts and travel (most: Edwin Lee $174,651, London N. Breed $148,816, Rafael Mandelman $50,845). In 227 of 872 official-and-source pairs the payor, recipient or giver also has recorded business with the same official: a lobbyist’s contact on its behalf, a sponsored file naming it, or campaign money. 29 further requested-payment rows were filed by department heads and other elected officers and are not shown here.
how: Requested (“behested”) payments are read from three Ethics Commission series: State Form 803 behested-payment reports (payments of 2015 to 2018), Form 3610b filings with their payors (2019 to 2021), and Form 114.5 reports of contributions to ballot committees made at an elected officer’s request (2019 to 2026). Gifts and travel are Form 700 Schedules D and E and the separate Gifts of Travel filings, with amended copies removed. Historical Form 803 amounts come from reviewed scans and their itemized schedules, including in-kind valuations. Form 3610b excludes recipient allocations and superseded payments. The committee total counts a receipt once across officers, and each named officer retains their attribution. Rows are grouped by official, source and recipient; a payor or giver who is a private individual is counted and shown as “a private party (not named)”. “Business before the official” looks the payor, recipient or giver up, by exact name, among clients in lobbyists’ reported contacts with that official, counterparties of passed money files the official sponsored, and donors to the official’s committees.
limits: Being connected is not being corrupt. Asking donors to support a charity or a civic event must be reported, which is why it is visible here; the Ethics Commission’s table lists 29 waivers of the behested-payment rules that the Board has approved. Only reported payments appear, and the State Form 803 series on disk stops in 2018, so totals by official are not comparable across eras. A payor with business before the official may have given for reasons that have nothing to do with it.
